content:
"Sir, you've advised the accused about his legal rights...Congratulations, you're now a co-accused." If this had been a courtroom joke, it would've landed perfectly. Unfortunately, it came from an Investigating Officer.

If litigation has taught me one thing, it is that sometimes the law needs to be explained to the very people entrusted with enforcing it. A few days ago, while pursuing a matter before a district court outside Delhi in the NCR, a colleague of mine received an interesting phone call from the Investigating Officer, an ASI in the State Police.

The allegation? The police had found chats between my colleague and an accused who was in judicial custody. According to the IO, because my colleague had discussed legal rights, possible remedies, and the preparation of a defence, he too had become a participant in the crime. A notice from the Police Station, he was informed, would shortly follow.

Quite an innovative interpretation of criminal jurisprudence. There was just one tiny problem. The alleged offence had taken place in 2024. At that point, my colleague had never met the accused, had never spoken to him, and had certainly never been appointed as his counsel. There wasn't a single piece of material connecting him with the alleged offence.

His only "crime" was accepting a vakalatnama after the incident and doing precisely what every advocate is professionally and constitutionally expected to do—advise his client. Apparently, in someone's legal universe, preparing a defence had become evidence of participating in the offence.

One also wonders what purpose Sections 132 and 134 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 serve if every privileged conversation between a lawyer and a client is treated as suspicious. Lawyer-client privilege is not a courtesy extended by the police; it is a statutory protection recognised by law.

After what turned into an unplanned lecture on criminal law, professional ethics, and privileged communication, the Investigating Officer eventually realised that pressure tactics may unsettle an ordinary citizen, but they don't work very well on advocates who spend their lives reading the statute book. The proposed "notice" quietly disappeared. 

An apology, however, did make an appearance.

Incidents like these are amusing in hindsight, but they also carry a serious reminder. The day an advocate starts fearing prosecution for advising clients is the day citizen's right to a fair defence begins to erode. Lawyers are not accessories to crimes because they defend the accused. If that were the law, every courtroom in the country would have far fewer advocates and far more empty chairs.

While hearing all this, I was taken back to a line that I had read somewhere "Litigation teaches you to stand up with your head held high, to protect your rights, when the world tells you to sit down"

Sometimes, the most important case an advocate argues is not for a client. It is for the Rule of Law itself.

comment: The larger concern is the chilling effect on defence strategy. Misreading legitimate advocacy as complicity can quietly discourage lawyers from challenging state action and weaken procedural safeguards.
